newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Chinese co satisfied with revolutionary NZ engine.
newsitem.headline: Chinese co satisfied with revolutionary NZ engine.

text.p: A Chinese firm said on Tuesday it was satisfied with a revolutionary New Zealand-designed engine and is preparing to finalise a deal.

Sichuan DongHua Machinery Works (SDMW) has signed a memorandum of understanding with the tiny New Zealand firm, Continuous Cycle Engine Development (CCED), and expects to complete the deal around July.
Although neither CCED nor SDMW would comment on the price to be paid, company sources suggest the deal could be worth hundreds of millions of NZ dollars.

CCED's Graeme Jenkins, co-investor of the engine, said big name international companies including Mitsui had expressed interest in the engine, which Jenkins said outperforms conventional motors on virtually every measure.

"Our engineers think this engine has new and unique principles and construction," director of SDMW Shi Zhongsang told Reuters while in New Zealand on an inspection visit and to meet Industry Minister John Luxton.
"It has a lot of advantages such as its very low weight and few parts. It is very easy to be made and very cheap," he said through an interpreter.
"We think the work CCED has done is a revolution in engine technology," Zhongsang said, adding that his firm's involvement was backed by the central Chinese government.
While the engine needed some further tests on fuel consumption and running life, SDMW was confident overall.
"After we have seen this engine, we have seen all we want to see and we know all we want to know. We have enough confidence in the technology," he said.
The engine has been sent to Auckland University for tests on consumption and life expectancy.

Jenkins says the engine has an arm-length list of superior qualities over conventional engines including lightness, power-to-weight performance, fuel consumption, emissions, vibration-free, lack of moving parts and ease of manufacture.

A prototype "Smitkin" made of aluminium weighs around 24 kg against a a similar combustion engine of 140 kg and is about the size of a car wheel. The diesel version has only 30 moving parts against around 4,000 in a current four cyclinder diesel.

State-owned SDMW, which also operates as a research institute with 180 engineers and technicians, said it planned to use the engine in cars, trucks, motorcycles, agricultural vehicles, generators, water pumps and boats.
"We think if everything goes smoothly it will take about one year for the first application to be commercialised," said Zhongsang.
SDMW currently has annual sales of US$30 million and among other things operates a medium-density fibre board plant using Malaysian technology.
It would produce engines for both the domestic market and for exports where export credits would be won.
"We think we will invest big capital in this project," said Zhongsang.
Part of the capital may come via Hong Kong. Licensing for production of the Smitkin will bought by a joint venture company, between SDMW and private Malaysian firm Pacific Base.

Pacific Base's David Lau said it would raise funds through the Hong Kong market, possibly via a public vehicle and funds would be used to pay for the licence and the establishment of manufacturing plants.
A meeting of interested fund managers has been called in Hong Kong for July 15-16. The handover of Hong Kong to China has delayed the signing of a deal, Lau said.
